newsitem.title: UK: NYMEX looks for changes in LME U.S. warehouses.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX looks for changes in LME U.S. warehouses.

text.p: Changes in U.S. futures industry legislation, possible next year, would make London Metal Exchange (LME) warehouses in the U.S. much more accountable to U.S. domestic scrutiny, Nymex Chairman Daniel Rappaport said.

"The LME generates a substantial amount of arbitrage volume...to the extent that the LME has warehouses in the U.S. they will have to comply with domestic rules and regulations," Rappaport told reporters at a briefing here.
Amongst proposed legislation in the U.S. Senate and Congress are proposals that would subject certain foreign commodity contracts to Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) regulatory authority.

Rappaport said the Sumitomo affair in June underscored misgivings and concerns that the New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX) had pointed out for a couple of years - most notably the U.S. warehouses for copper.
Sumitomo said in June that it had lost $1.8 billion, subsequently revised up to $2.6 billion, in ten years of unauthorised copper trading by its former head trader Yasuo Hamanaka.

John Moore, Chairman of the COMEX Governers Committee Copper Advisory Committee, said that at one point during the height of the affair some 80,000 tonnes of copper were attracted to the LME's Long Beach warehouse to the detriment of U.S. consumers.
Because the LME delivery points in the U.S. were not subject to U.S. legislation, the CFTC was unable to inquire over large positions or use position limits, Rappaport said.
"When any industry seeks to bring products into the U.S., they are compelled to follow U.S. regulations," he said.
Automobile makers and pharmaceutical manufacturers, for example, have to comply with U.S. environmental laws and medicinal legislation.
"Compelling the LME to follow CFTC rules is not extra-territoriality - it is fair that the LME should follow CFTC rules," he said.
Because this is not so, the U.S. domestic exchanges are operating at a competitive disadvantage.
The bill that will be before the next session of Congress after the U.S. Presidential election would require owners of materials in U.S. warehouses to provide information to the CFTC.
But this would not mean that ownership would become "common knowledge'. Rather, filtered information would pass to the relevant exchange.
"In the best of all worlds we would not be advocating more legislation on the LME. In the best of all worlds we would be advocating less legislation in domestic exchanges," Rappaport said.
The two issues that Congress should consider is position accountability and position limits, although the latter is not as crucial as the former, he said.

Such legislation, if enacted, would not only apply to the LME in the U.S., but also some of the domestic markets. The CSCE has delivery points overseas and the CME also has contracts listed in other countries, he noted.
